name: Lemborexant

lead: Lemborexant (Dayvigo) is a prescription insomnia medicine from the orexin-antagonist class. It is approved for adults who have trouble falling or staying asleep.
It has not been tested for any appearance effect. Any link to looksmaxxing is through the general idea that sleep supports recovery.

paras: It blocks orexin receptors OX1R and OX2R, which reduces the wake-promoting signal in the brain, rather than boosting GABA like benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.

Reported effects include sleepiness, headache and abnormal dreams; the label also warns of next-day impairment, sleep paralysis, complex sleep behaviors and worsening depression. It is prescription-only and Schedule IV in the US.

lead: Lemborexant, sold as Dayvigo, is a prescription oral medicine for adults with insomnia involving trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It was developed by Eisai and belongs to the dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA) class, which blocks the wake-promoting orexin (hypocretin) signalling system rather than enhancing GABA activity as benzodiazepines and Z-drugs do.[1][2]

The US Food and Drug Administration approved it in December 2019, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the United States.[1] Phase 3 trials have compared it with placebo and with zolpidem extended-release in older adults, and a 12-month trial has reported longer-term efficacy and tolerability data.[3][4]

Lemborexant has no approved cosmetic or appearance indication, and no published study has tested it for appearance outcomes. Its relevance to looksmaxxing discussions is indirect, through the wider topic of sleep quality and recovery. Reported adverse effects include somnolence, headache, and abnormal dreams, and its label carries warnings about next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors.[2]

paras: The US label indicates lemborexant for adults with insomnia characterised by difficulty with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance.[2] Safety and effectiveness have not been established in children.[1]

Lemborexant is not approved or studied for any cosmetic purpose. Within looksmaxxing and recovery discussions, sleep is generally treated as a background factor for appearance and health, and sleep medicines are occasionally mentioned in that context; published research on lemborexant concerns sleep outcomes only.[5]

The label states that lemborexant is presumed to act by antagonising orexin receptors OX1R and OX2R, blocking the binding of the wake-promoting neuropeptides orexin A and B and thereby suppressing wake drive.[2] In vitro characterisation studies describe it as a competitive dual receptor antagonist.[6]

Grokipedia reports peak plasma concentrations about one to three hours after oral dosing and an elimination half-life of roughly 17 to 19 hours; the drug is mainly metabolised by CYP3A enzymes, so the label advises dose limits or avoidance with CYP3A inhibitors and inducers.[1][2]

The label lists somnolence or fatigue, headache, and nightmares or abnormal dreams among the most common adverse reactions, and warns about CNS-depressant effects with possible next-day impairment, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, cataplexy-like symptoms, complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking, worsening depression or suicidal ideation, and caution in people with compromised respiratory function.[2] The label notes that no pregnancy data are available to evaluate risk and refers clinicians to a pregnancy registry.[2] It is contraindicated in narcolepsy.[1]

A phase 2 Bayesian adaptive dose-finding study in adults and older adults used polysomnography to assess sleep efficiency, latency to persistent sleep, and wake after sleep onset, alongside next-morning sleepiness.[7] A phase 3 trial in people aged 55 and over compared lemborexant with placebo and with zolpidem extended-release.[3] SUNRISE 2, a 12-month trial of 949 randomised adults with insomnia, had a six-month placebo-controlled period followed by an active-treatment period.[4] Grokipedia summarises the pivotal trials as showing improvements over placebo in sleep latency, wake after sleep onset and sleep efficiency.[1]

Network meta-analyses have compared lemborexant with other insomnia drugs, including suvorexant and a broad set of hypnotics, and reviewers have noted limits in long-term comparative data.[8][9] Other registered studies are examining lemborexant in sleep-wake rhythm disorder with Alzheimer disease, and in insomnia among people with chronic pain.[10][11] All of these concern sleep, not appearance.

Lemborexant is sold under the brand name Dayvigo.[2] Looksmaxxing forums include few discussions of it specifically; orexin antagonists are mostly mentioned, if at all, as part of general talk about sleep aids and sleep quality.

timeline.event: A phase 2 dose-finding study of lemborexant is published.[7]
FDA approves lemborexant (Dayvigo) for adult insomnia.[1]
SUNRISE 2 reports results from a 6-month placebo-controlled period of a 12-month trial.[4]
